runs.text: When I was younger, the world called me by names that never fit bipolar, borderline, broken, out of control. No one thought “autism.” I had already learned to mask so well—copy, perform, survive—that even I didn’t suspect it. I could give speeches, light up a room, then collapse for two days afterward in silence. That wasn’t weakness. That was autistic burnout.

Later, when I finally told a doctor I thought I might be autistic, he didn’t hesitate before dismissing me. “No. You can’t be. Autistic people don’t have empathy.” That’s when I knew he was wrong. Empathy has always been my superpower and my curse. I feel everything too much. I burn out carrying what isn’t mine. And when I hyperfocus on something—when I dive in until the rest of the world fades—that isn’t a distraction. That’s me most alive.

Autism reframed everything. It explained the overwhelm, the masking, the loneliness, and the strange brilliance of noticing what others missed. For years I believed I was defective. What I see now is that I was misnamed. Autism doesn’t erase my capacity to connect. It redefines it.
And still, the system punished me anyway. At twenty, I walked away from an abusive marriage only to land back in my mother’s house. Pills, lies, and survival games. I was arrested for five
counts of prescription
fraud. The truth didn’t matter. They gave me three years in prison. Not minimum security, either—maximum. Because of my anger. Because I had learned early that showing weakness was lethal.

Prison taught me what CPS already had: the world will mislabel you, misdiagnose you, and then punish you for the mask you had to wear just to survive. I did my time. I fought, I endured, I refused to vanish. But release wasn’t redemption. It was another kind of return—
coming back to a world that still didn’t understand me and rebuilding anyway.

So, when I say “return,” I don’t just mean walking out of a cell. I mean walking back into my own life with new language, new clarity, and no apology. The return is the moment you stop accepting the names other people gave you. It’s when you see yourself clearly, maybe for the first time, and you stay.
Because people like me don’t need fixing. We need to see. We need space to stop masking. And maybe most of all—we need permission to finally accept ourselves.
I don’t wish to fight against this life anymore.
Not the way it keeps twisting.
Not the way people leave without warning.
Not the way my own thoughts split me into pieces.
I have carried every label they gave me
until my shoulders weren’t mine
just storage units for judgment.
But today,
I let go.
Of needing to fix you.
Of needing to explain me.
Of needing anything, really,
except breath and maybe some grace.
Love doesn’t mean agreement.
Kindness doesn’t require approval.
Truth doesn’t beg to be believed.
We are all just trying to make it,
and some of us have already died a hundred times
before the day even begins.
So no,
I won’t play God with your life.
I won’t weaponize my healing
to measure your pain.
I’ll be here.
Just me.
Choosing again.
Because every day is a decision:
Will I harden or soften?
Will I guard or give?
Will I stay small or burn holy?
What will I choose today?
And can I live with that answer?
Opening balance: steady.
Morning quiet +20.
Surprise meeting −30.
Deep work win +25.
Fluorescent room −40.
Walk and water +10.
Phone scroll −15.
Closing balance: enough to make dinner.
On my skin is the truth I could never speak aloud:
What nourishes me also destroys me.
I inked it there for her, for the woman whose love was both milk and poison. My mother has always been my first home and my first fire.
She gave me life and yet scorched me with it. She placed me in the flames, over and over, and still I crawled back to her warmth. Her love was a shelter with a burning
roof,
a feast laced with hunger. I have never stopped being confounded by her, how the same hands that held me could also push me into the dark.
And yet, my love for her never wavered. That is the part that feels most impossible: that I could stand in the ashes of what she burned down and still love her without condition.
Forgiveness was always simple; it flowed as naturally as breath. Trust, though, that is the fracture that will not mend. Trust is what died between us and will not be reborn.

But here, at the end of all the burning, I can bring gratitude. Gratitude for the pieces of her love that did nourish me. Gratitude for the fire itself, because it tempered me, carved me into something stronger, stranger, more alive even.
She is the paradox at my core: my undoing and my making. My greatest wound, and the root I will never sever. To return to her is to return to the fire yes but this time, I do not fear the flames.
